title: Mango Diplomacy: How India's Embassies Are Making America Fall for the King of Fruits
excerpt: From Costco aisles to Dupont Circle tents, Indian mangoes are selling out faster than they arrive — powered by NRI nostalgia and a quiet diplomatic push.
body:
From Dupont Circle in Washington to Union Square in Manhattan, Indian mangoes are starring in what may be the sweetest diplomatic offensive America has ever tasted.

On Saturday, the Indian Embassy in Washington partners with the Dupont Circle Business Improvement District for the second straight year to offer free Alphonso, Kesar, and Langra mangoes, mango lassis, and cultural programming in Dupont Circle Park — a sunlit afternoon of fruit, DJ sets, and soft power. The event caps a week in which Indian consulates from Seattle to New York staged similar festivals, drawing thousands of Americans and homesick NRIs into lines that wrapped around city blocks.

## More Than a Fruit Stand

In New York, the Consulate General hosted an Indian Mango Festival at Union Square that drew more than 1,000 tasters despite intermittent rain. Two varieties — Kesar from Gir and Langra from Varanasi — disappeared almost as fast as volunteers could slice them.

"Indian mango is popular and gaining a lot of attention here. Everywhere people are talking about them — there is immense enthusiasm for mangoes from India," Deputy Consul General Vishal Harsh told reporters. The Consulate plans to expand the event next year with more varieties and larger venues.

For many in the crowd, the tasting was more than curiosity. "It brings back memories of having mangoes with my whole family," one attendee said. "I'm going to take a photograph of the mangoes and send it to my mother." Another, a young Indian-American woman, broke down in tears after her first bite. "These remind me of my grandmother," she said. "It has been almost 10 years since I've had Indian mangoes in India. This is like gold."

## A $40 Box of Nostalgia

The emotion is not incidental — it is, increasingly, the market itself. Indian mango exports to the United States reached $10 million in the 2023-24 fiscal year, more than double the $4.36 million recorded the year before. At Costco, Kesar mangoes sell out within hours of arriving on shelves. Executive Bob Huskey told trade media they are "selling faster than we can bring them back in."

A box of 10 to 12 Indian mangoes retails for roughly $40 — a price point that puts the fruit on par with lobster tails. But as one industry executive told The Packer, "it's not a rational purchase. It is more an emotional purchase. The Indian diaspora is a very affluent community. They can spend more for good food. And this is one thing they can proudly claim is their heritage."

Kesar has quietly overtaken Alphonso as the dominant export variety. While Alphonso remains more coveted — its floral sweetness is the stuff of monsoon mythology — it is also more delicate and yields inconsistent results after the long journey to American shelves. Kesar, sturdier and more forgiving, now accounts for roughly half of all Indian mango imports.

## Mango Diplomacy, Literally

India's Ambassador to the United States, Vinay Kwatra, explicitly framed the push as diplomatic strategy. "We all have a sense of diaspora nostalgia when it comes to mango," he told IANS. "Summer vacations remind us of the times when we would enjoy mango to our heart's content. But we are now facing a very happy situation where this nostalgia is now available with American retailers."

The concerted embassy effort draws a direct line to what diplomats call "mango diplomacy" — a phrase that dates back to George W. Bush's 2006 visit to India, when the American president tasted an Alphonso mango and reportedly declared it "a hell of a fruit." That visit opened the door for the first commercial shipments.

Nearly two decades later, Indian consulates are hosting tasting events in partnership with APEDA, the government's agricultural export body, and wooing major retailers from Costco to H Mart. In Seattle, the Consul General brought together more than 100 importers, distributors, and retail executives for a "Mango Magic" showcase of seven premium varieties.

## What's Next

The mango festivals are only the beginning. With the US mango import market now exceeding $1 billion in annual value, India is eyeing a far larger slice. The immediate challenge is supply chain and shelf life — getting fragile Alphonsos to American kitchens in peak condition — but the demand signal is unmistakable. For the 4.8 million Indian Americans spread across the country, a mango is never just a mango. It is a summer in Ratnagiri, a grandmother's kitchen, a childhood measured in sticky fingers and sweet juice. And now, it is available at Costco.
